You don't have sufficient data to consider such a complex model. Even if you don't object to this on philosophical grounds, I'm sure you have a basic identifiability problem with only 25 detections in the data set.  You could track this down by building the model stepwise from the null model (having no covariates) and find out "when the data run out"

regards
andy

You should use NA to indicate missing values in your data set. An other option is using the na.strings argument in read.table( ) when importing your data set and setting it to read.table(, na.strings = "-").

Also be sure to use the most recent version of AICcmodavg.

Let me know if the problem persists,

Marc

Hi Richard,

Not sure if this will give you (or anyone else) any other ideas, but I figured I'd throw it out there....

Earlier, I was referring to the mean estimate for p(detection).  I calculated p(det) using the covariate levels at each station and averaged across stations.  Anyway, my pcount estimates were a mess.

After all that, I tried to get things going in pcountOpen ('PCO'), reasoning that many of the problems I was experiencing in pcount might be due (as others suggested) to a closure violation.  I treated each visit as a primary period.  I think my PCO models look a lot more realistic compared to the pcount models.  I didn't add any covariates for recruitment or survival, potentially that could improve things some more.

My Indigo Bunting / clearcuts PCO model is giving me NaNs, but none of the other models I selected (using forward selection) are doing that.

Hi Marcia,

your model is composed of two logistic regressions for occupancy (psi) and detection (p) for site i and rep j:

logit(psi_i) = beta0 + beta1 * cov1 + etc               # model for occupancy
logit(p_ij) = alpha0 + alpha1 * cov1 + etc              # model for detection

Function occu() picks values of parameters alpha0, alpha1, beta0, beta1, etc.... that are optimal according to the ML criterion. Function predict() plugs these param estimates into the linear model, backtransforms from the logit scale to the probability scale (if you choose so) and uses the delta rule to get the uncertainty of these predictions (SE and CI). This is done separately for both parts of the model. So regardless of whether you have a detection covariate or not, predict() simply takes the occupancy parameter estimates and computes psi from them, using the covariate values that you provide in the new.data argument.

>From your output below, the param estimates under the two models differ. Hence, it seems impossible to me that you get the same predictions for occupancy under the two models.

???

Dear Camille,
 It makes sense that estimates of abundance should vary quite a bit once you start explaining heterogeneity in detection probability. That makes sense to me.

 As for "p" changing so much among models, the interpretation of that is based on the intercept of the model for logit(p) and how the covariates are defined. Are they categorical levels or continuous? Are they standardized?  If they are categorical ("factors") then the interpretation of p is at the baseline level (the summary output should make this clear). If they are continuous but not standardized then the interpretation is at the value "x = 0", so you should probably standardize each continuous covariate.

 Does p = 0.27 seem reasonable?  Keep in mind that this is INDIVIDUAL level p and not SURVEY level p.  For example, if there are N = 2 groups then the "survey level" p is :   1- (1-0.27)^2  = 0.47 or, in general,   1-(1-0.27)^N
which will be much higher.

regards,
andy

I am indeed happy to see that unmarked is now the dominant detection
probability estimation software. Nice work everyone!
A few comments on this issue, the blog post, comments to that, and
previous incarnations of the whole thing:

1. The discussion at the blog seems to center around scolding of Dan
Linden for suggesting that unbiasedness is a virtuous property. Yet
these scolds don't really publish anything in the ecological
literature proclaiming the great virtues of minimizing variance to the
detriment of producing biased estimators, at least that I've seen.

2. I find the support for using biased estimators pretty
surprising. It doesn't seem to be a prevailing view. Why is that?  I
know someone will pull the "MLE of a normal variance" card on me, but
I can't remember the last time I've seen someone interested in
inference about a normal variance.

3. The counter-example is "shrinkage estimators" and related
things. But these are almost universally applied to extremely
high-dimensional estimation problems or problems that are
unstable. They are not routinely (if ever) applied in hypothesis
driven research, and I think this is a key point missed by the
discussants.

I know people will pull the "but this is the same as a Bayesian's
prior" card on me. But in the context of prior specification, as a
matter of standard practice, no one intentionally chooses a prior to
impose information (and hence frequentist bias) unless a parameter is
poorly identified.

4. But all of this is really a distraction and misses the big point,
which is: what is the ecological process that is the focus of
inference?  The use of an occupancy model clearly identifies that
objective as "probability of occurrence" which I think is often a
reasonable thing to develop models for. But what about Brian McGill
and these guys? Would they claim the object of inference to be the
product p*psi?  If this is such a good thing, how come no one ever
states upfront that p*psi is the target of their inference? Think
about that: what if we claim to do science about some ecological
process, but then never declare what that process is? Does that make
sense? To me it does not.

By saying it's really great to have estimators of p*psi that have low
MSE, then what problem in ecological science does this help you solve?
So you estimate thing A with less variability than someone else
estimates thing B. But it seems relevant what thing A and thing B are
and whether one of them is more relevant to the scientific or
management question being asked.

This has nothing to do about "detectability", nothing even about
statistics, but is really more of a basic conceptual or philosophical
issue. What system are we studying, what is our objective, what is a
sensible model of that system?  (and note that occupancy models are a
model of the system, not some black-box for generating estimators of
some meaningless parameter).

Dan's comment to the post seems mostly about this issue and not
really what should be virtuous properties of estimators.

5. There are now many papers (and blog entries) which scold people for
"detectability". Any statistician could make a living by writing such
papers -- simply take any procedure, find where it breaks, and then
hold that situation up as the evidence against doing it (and write a
paper scolding the users). But this evidence doesn't support the
alternative, or any specific alternative for the simple reason that we
know, without doing ANY analysis, that any statistical procedure will
not function well uniformly over all conditions.  Understanding
performance over a range of conditions is useful for designing studies
in which we aim to use the procedure but there is no logical basis for
dismissing the whole procedure because we identify some conditions
where it breaks down.  (unless you are against all of statistics which is
not an argument I'm seeing anyone make).

So we have an example of this: People use occupancy models for making
inferences about psi (see point 4 above), Welsh et al. write a paper
demonstrating some unfavorable conditions and it is then used to
dismiss the whole idea of occupancy models.  "here are some cases
where, for an estimator of some thing, and by some objective function,
we do better by not accounting for detection probability and therefore
the detection probability guys are wrong!"  Instead, this could at
best be interpreted as being relevant to study design and not the
model of the system (occupancy), unless someone has a coherent
argument to support the virtues of inference about "p*psi". i.e., what
ecological problem does it solve?

6. Summary: It is preferable to focus on clear statements of
objectives and building sensible models for ecological systems (which
we normally have to observe by taking samples of individuals, of
spatial locations, of species, etc.). Does some methodological
framework describe your system and facilitate inference about some
quantity that gives a clear interpretation to your scientific or management
question? Then use it.

> So you estimate thing A with less variability than someone else
> estimates thing B. But it seems relevant what thing A and thing B are
> and whether one of them is more relevant to the scientific or
> management question being asked.
>
> This has nothing to do about "detectability", nothing even about
> statistics, but is really more of a basic conceptual or philosophical
> issue. What system are we studying, what is our objective, what is a
> sensible model of that system?  (and note that occupancy models are a
> model of the system, not some black-box for generating estimators of
> some meaningless parameter).
>
> Dan's comment to the post seems mostly about this issue and not
> really what should be virtuous properties of estimators.
>
> 5. There are now many papers (and blog entries) which scold people for
> "detectability". Any statistician could make a living by writing such
> papers -- simply take any procedure, find where it breaks, and then
> hold that situation up as the evidence against doing it (and write a
> paper scolding the users). But this evidence doesn't support the
> alternative, or any specific alternative for the simple reason that we
> know, without doing ANY analysis, that any statistical procedure will
> not function well uniformly over all conditions.  Understanding
> performance over a range of conditions is useful for designing studies
> in which we aim to use the procedure but there is no logical basis for
> dismissing the whole procedure because we identify some conditions
> where it breaks down.  (unless you are against all of statistics which is
> not an argument I'm seeing anyone make).
>
> So we have an example of this: People use occupancy models for making
> inferences about psi (see point 4 above), Welsh et al. write a paper
> demonstrating some unfavorable conditions and it is then used to
> dismiss the whole idea of occupancy models.  "here are some cases
> where, for an estimator of some thing, and by some objective function,
> we do better by not accounting for detection probability and therefore
> the detection probability guys are wrong!"  Instead, this could at
> best be interpreted as being relevant to study design and not the
> model of the system (occupancy), unless someone has a coherent
> argument to support the virtues of inference about "p*psi". i.e., what
> ecological problem does it solve?
>
> 6. Summary: It is preferable to focus on clear statements of
> objectives and building sensible models for ecological systems (which
> we normally have to observe by taking samples of individuals, of
> spatial locations, of species, etc.). Does some methodological
> framework describe your system and facilitate inference about some
> quantity that gives a clear interpretation to your scientific or management
> question? Then use it.

Thank you,
Sinead

I think as we all know having a single number such as mean square error to represent what's going on in complex situations just doesn't tell the whole story.  To illustrate that I've attached an animated gif file (which can be viewed in any web browser) showing a "histogram-type" display for the distributions of the naïve, maximum likelihood, and Bayesian posterior mean estimators of psi (probability of presence).  (The actual distributions are, of course, very discrete but binning things and summing the probabilities into the appropriate bin can be a reasonable visual summary.)

Just for creating an example I set psi = 0.75 and varied the detection probability (p) from 0.01 to 0.99 and set the sample size to 55 sites with 2 visits to each site.  The Bayesian estimator uses uniform priors for both psi and p.  The dark gray bar that sometimes shows in the maximum likelihood figure represents the probability that the maximum likelihood estimator is exactly 1.0 (which can have a very high probability of occurring).  The dotted line in each of the 3 sub-figures shows where psi = 0.75 is.  If there is interest, I can construct similar examples with different settings.
